verdict.reasoning: Patient reports: "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment. I got stung by a wasp recently..." and confirms sting was "just a few minutes ago."

Sting: "I got stung by a wasp... one of the two" (bee/wasp). Location: "Yeah, it was on my arm." Rash/redness/puncture: "I've got a bit of a rash on my arm where I got stung" and later "It's slightly red... there's a bit of a... hole where... the puncture mark." Blotchy rash: "just a bit kind of blotchy and a bit of a rash." Arm side (right) is not specified in transcript, so that portion is an unstated detail but does not contradict.
Patient states: "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment" and later clarifies it is not particularly acute, consistent with mild breathing difficulty.
Patient reports: "potentially there's a bit of swelling in my lips and tongue. Feels a bit weird."
Patient says they are "feeling like slightly anxious" and later: "I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse. I just wanted to speak to someone."
When asked about anxiety/panic: Patient answers, "Yeah, sometimes. Occasionally."
On history of anaphylaxis: Patient replies, "Not that I know of, no."
When asked about EpiPen: Patient says, "I haven't, no."
Past medical history: "I've had eczema before. That's kind of the major thing."
Regarding meds for this event: "Not at the moment, no. Nothing. Nothing yet."
On psychiatric meds: When asked if ever been on medication for anxiety/panic, patient responds, "No. No." indicating no regular psychiatric medications.
Allergy history: Patient states, "I'm allergic to penicillin."
Social history: In response to work: "I am a computer scientist."
Living situation: When asked, "And you're living alone?" patient answers, "Yes."
Pets: When asked, "Do you have any pets at home?" patient replies, "I have a cat."

Doctor observes: "Your breathing seems all right to me right now" and later: "based on how you look, how you're talking to me and how you're breathing... Thankfully you don't have anything like [stridor] right now."

Exam: "your lips don't seem swollen to me right now" and after oral exam: no mention of swelling and assessment states no life-threatening reaction; consistent with no observed lip/oral soft-tissue swelling.

Arm exam: Doctor: "That looks okay to me... Does it look red to you..." Patient: "It's slightly red... there's a bit of a... hole where... the puncture mark" and "just a bit kind of blotchy and a bit of a rash. It doesn't feel like particularly swollen." No warmth is described; thus no significant swelling/warmth observed.

Doctor: "it seems to me that this is a localized allergic reaction" and assessment focuses on wrist/arm with statement: "I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction" and no systemic signs described.

While anxiety and occasional panic are acknowledged and the patient feels anxious, the clinician does not explicitly state that anxiety-related dyspnea or panic is contributing to breathlessness; this is an interpretive addition not directly made in the transcript.
Penicillin allergy is both elicited ("I'm allergic to penicillin") and implicitly carried into assessment; describing it as a historical problem matches the transcript.
Plan: "What I'd like you to do now... is I'd like you to try and take some antihistamines... That should be enough to control this."
Doctor: "you can get pyritone or chlorphenamine and you can take one tablet, four milligrams, up to about six times a day."
Doctor: "Or you can just take a one a day. Whichever is your preference, that's absolutely fine."
Regarding obtaining medication: "you can buy [over] the counter... Any chemist will have it... You don't need a prescription for that."

Doctor advises: "If the redness in your arm spreads and it feels hot or, you know, you have signs of any localised infection, we may need to think about other treatments..." which implies monitoring for spread, increasing redness, warmth, or pain/infection.
Same segment: "we may need to think about other treatments like an antibiotic" if signs of localized infection develop.

Doctor explains red-flag signs: swelling of lips, difficulty breathing, stridor, and rapidly progressing symptoms, and instructs to go to A&E if these occur: "if anything deteriorates... go straight to ae... in some cases, if it's progressing rapidly, it's better to go straight to AE."

Doctor: "if anything changes, if anything deteriorates, either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae... if it's progressing rapidly, it's better to go straight to AE rather than to wait for a booked appointment with us" and also "have a low threshold for having a chat with us."

Doctor: "on the basis of what you told me, I don't think you need any allergy testing... However, if it was to happen that... you're having these kind of reactions on a regular basis or other non specific rashes, you might need to think about blood testing."

Reassurance and info: "I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction" and later: "I'm going to leave some information about anaphylactic reactions just for you to read about it. I don't want you to panic, but just for you to be aware..."

Doctor advises: "if anything deteriorates in terms of your breathing... someone actually needs to be taken urgently" and at end: "Come back to us if you have any further issues." This covers return/worsening or new concerning features.

Follow-up advice: "if anything deteriorates... either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae... if it's progressing rapidly, it's better to go straight to AE rather than to wait for a booked appointment" and "Just have a low threshold for having a chat with us."
Similar to plan-011: "if anything deteriorates..." and "Come back to us if you have any further issues" indicates return if symptoms worsen or new features develop.
